section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p: The Impression Document Description Format (DDF) is an ASCII, tagged-text format exported by Impression's Save text with styles operation. It transfers text together with style definitions and formatting. An Impression document is consequently represented as a linear stream: ordinary characters provide the content and brace-delimited commands provide structure, style and embedded non-ASCII characters. It is suitable for interchange and for programs which need to generate styled Impression text without constructing an Impression native file.

DDF is interpreted whenever text is loaded into a frame; it is also the intermediate representation used by Impression loaders. A file intended for ordinary text loading must therefore use {off} if it may contain brace sequences which must remain literal. The normal RISC OS file type registered for DDF is &D93. Some historical software has associated DDF with other file types, including &707, but new DDF files should use the registered type. ASCII files may also be interpreted as DDF when explicitly requested.

The format is deliberately seven-bit. Printable ASCII text is copied directly; commands encode the opening brace and characters outside the printable range. Writers should emit ASCII only, use the code command for character values 128 to 255, and define every non-resident style before applying it.

section.title: Terminology
section.p: Control element means a sequence beginning with { and ending with }. Attribute is a named style property in a definition, such as font or leftmargin. Effect is an attribute command in the text stream; supplying a value sets or overrides that property and omitting the value restores the value supplied by the active styles. A style is a named group of attributes. A ruler is a named formatting definition normally used for paragraph geometry. Rulers use the same attribute syntax as styles and exported files may include font, spacing, justification, menu and other attributes in them.

subsection.title: Byte stream and lexical rules
subsection.p: The file is a sequence of elements. Outside a control element, ASCII 32 to 126 is text except {. ASCII 9 is a tab; ASCII 10 and ASCII 13 each end a paragraph. Other control characters are ignored. The closing brace is ordinary text outside a command, but the opening brace must be written as {\ 123} (or {code 123}).

Within a control element, spaces and ASCII 10 are whitespace. Closing brace, semicolon, comma and characters below ASCII 33 delimit keywords and arguments. Keywords are case-insensitive. An identifier is a letter followed by letters or digits. A quoted string may contain printable ASCII other than its delimiting double quote and preserves case; use it for style and font names containing spaces. No escape convention is defined for a double quote within a string, so writers must not place one inside the value.

Arguments which are not restricted to identifiers may also be bare tokens. A bare token ends at whitespace or a command delimiter and may contain punctuation; font names such as Trinity.Medium.Italic use this form. It is not known whether style-name matching is case-sensitive in every version of Impression.

subsection.title: Command boundaries and disabled processing
subsection.p: Commands are normally one brace-delimited unit. A semicolon separates attributes in define. The closing brace terminates the control element. Control elements require no separator and are commonly written next to one another as {First off}{Second on}.

{off} disables DDF interpretation. All following bytes, including apparent commands, are text until {on} is met. The on/off commands remain recognised while disabled. A robust reader should preserve this state across the complete stream; a robust writer should avoid using disabled mode except for literal imported text.

subsection.title: Styles, rulers and scope
subsection.p: A style application has the forms {style name on}, {ruler name on}, {name on}, or the corresponding off form. The optional integer after the switch is its application level, counted from the top of the style list; zero inserts the application at the top, which is the normal position. Styles form an ordered active list. An off command removes the named application even when another style was applied after it, so styles need not be removed in last-in, first-out order. A style-on should be paired with a style-off, although Impression closes unmatched applications at document end.

p.fixme: A control element containing only a style name is syntactically valid, but the effect of that form is not known.

subsection.p: Applying an effect which sets an attribute replaces an earlier effect at the same attribute. A bare effect keyword cancels that effect and restores the value supplied by the active style applications.

{define style name [basedon base]; attributes} creates a named style. It takes no text-stream position itself. The style must precede its first application. define ruler has the same syntax, and may contain the full range of style attributes. Rulers are conventionally used for leftmargin, rightmargin, returnmargin, tabs and paragraph rules; effectruler distinguishes rulers used as effects. The format also permits a definition with an empty attribute list. Attributes are separated by semicolons; a definition may appear anywhere in loaded text.

basedon names a style from which the new definition inherits its initial attributes; attributes in the new definition then replace the inherited values. It is not known whether the base style may be defined later, or how missing and circular base-style references are handled.

subsection.title: Values

definition-table.definition: One or more decimal digits.
An optional sign followed by an unsigned integer.
An unsigned integer, optionally followed by a decimal point and digits.
A letter followed by zero or more letters or digits.
A double-quoted sequence of printable ASCII characters. No escape syntax for an embedded double quote is defined.
A bare token or quoted string naming a font family and face. Quote a name which contains whitespace or delimiters.

One or two measurements. A measurement is an unsigned real, optionally preceded by a minus sign, followed by an optional unit.
The purpose and interpretation of the optional second measurement are not known.

definition.name: Unit
definition.extra: m cm mm yd ft in pi pt, ", '"

definition-table.definition:
Metre, centimetre, millimetre, yard, foot, inch, pica and point respectively; double quote and apostrophe are inch and foot.
The unit used when the suffix is omitted is not defined.
Unsigned integer followed by percent sign.
Case-insensitive boolean keyword.

subsection.p: Twelve points make one pica; 72 points make one inch. Negative right margins are distances from the frame's right edge; positive right margins are positions measured from its left edge. Writers must retain the sign rather than normalising right-margin values.

subsection.title: Style attributes and effects
subsection.p: The following attributes are valid in a definition. Unless stated otherwise, the same keyword plus a value is an effect, and the bare keyword cancels it.

definition-table.definition: Font family and face name.
Text size.
Absolute line spacing.
Line spacing as a percentage of font size.
Space before and after paragraphs.
Conditional frame-throw threshold.
Paragraph left, right and first-line/return margins.

definition.name: ruleleftmargin; rulerightmargin; rulewidth; vertrulewidth; ruleaboveoffset; ruleoffset

definition-table.definition: Horizontal and vertical paragraph-rule geometry.

A measured keep-together setting.
The precise meaning of the measurement and its interaction with the boolean keep attributes are not known.
Text, background, line and rule colours.
Horizontal font aspect/scale.
Horizontal movement in thousandths of an em.
Paragraph alignment.
Tab stops and optional types.

Paragraph-rule control value.
The numeric values and their effects are not known.

definition.name: strikeout; hyphenate; menuitem; locktolinespace; bold; italic; keepparagraph; keepnext; keepregion; overprint; overprintb; effectruler

definition-table.definition: Boolean formatting, menu, keep and ruler controls. overprintb is background overprint.
Baseline script mode.

Underline mode. off and zero disable underlining.
The meanings of the remaining numeric underline values are not fully known.
Tab leader text.
Character used by decimal tabs.
Marks an index entry.
Contents level.
Flag requesting automatic line spacing.

Marks a style or ruler as participating in automatic paragraph processing. It is emitted without an argument.
The complete automatic-paragraph behaviour controlled by this attribute is not known.
Style-menu shortcut identifier.

A bare style name is permitted as a style-definition attribute.
The meaning of a bare style name in an attribute list is not known.

subsection.title: Tabs, colours and numbering
subsection.p: tabs takes one or more comma-separated tab specifications. Each is an optional type followed by a measurement. Types are left, centre, right, decimal and vertrule; omitting the type means left. Each subsequent tab specification is separated by a comma. leader gives the tab leader string and dectabchar gives the character used to align decimal tabs.

A colour specification is rgb=(r,g,b), cmyk=(c,m,y,k), hsv=(h,s,v), or rgb24=(r,g,b). RGB, CMYK and HSV components normally range from 0 to 1, except HSV hue ranges from 0 to 360; RGB24 components range from 0 to 255. These colour specifications may be used by fontcolour, backcolour, linecolour and rulecolour.

pagenumber and chapternumber insert the applicable number. Their optional display form is decimal, romanlower or romanupper; an unsigned integer is also syntactically allowed. No argument means normal decimal display.

p.fixme: The grammar also names roman and upperroman forms, and does not define the meaning of an unsigned integer number specification. The accepted aliases and numeric meanings require confirmation.

definition-table.definition: Inserts a tab; raw ASCII 9 is equivalent.
Ends a paragraph; raw ASCII 10 or 13 is equivalent.
Inserts the character with that numeric code. Use for opening brace and 8-bit characters.
Inserts literal wildcard characters for DDF used by search/replace.
Inserts a discretionary hyphen.
Applies x and y movement to following text, in thousandths of an em.
Forces subsequent text into the next frame.

subsection.title: Version-dependent and unresolved commands
subsection.p: Different Impression-family versions extended the original command set. A reader may encounter the following controls in addition to the core grammar. Tools which cannot interpret an extension should preserve its complete control element when round-tripping a file.

definition-table.definition:
Defines named colours and tints.
The complete record syntax, component ranges, tint syntax and name-escaping rules are not known.

Inserts or identifies a mail-merge field.
The exact argument grammar and evaluation rules are not known.

Control the size and baseline offset of subscript and superscript text.
The argument types, units and reset forms are not known.

Control line decoration size and offset.
The argument types, units and affected line decorations are not known.

Controls automatic indentation.
The argument grammar and behaviour are not known.

Places a box or rule around a paragraph. The optional number is in the range 1 to 3 and selects formatting flags.
The precise appearance of each form, the default number and the meanings of values 1 to 3 are not known.

Starts automatic paragraph numbering using the given numbering type and initial number. Type zero produces decimal numbering and type one produces upper-case Roman numerals.
The remaining numbering-type values are not known.

Inserts the next automatic paragraph number using the specified numbering type.
The complete numbering-type table is not known.

subsection.p: Unknown commands cannot safely be discarded: they may define formatting which is not represented elsewhere in the stream. A lossless transformer should retain each unknown brace-delimited control element at its original position.

item.p: Encode source text as seven-bit ASCII. Emit raw printable characters except opening brace; emit tabs and paragraph ends in their raw or command forms.
Emit define style and define ruler commands before their first uses, with semicolon-separated attributes and quoted names where needed.

Maintain an ordered set of active named styles. Emit a matching off command for each style-on command; an off command may remove a style which is not the most recently applied. Use a zero or absent level unless deliberately selecting a lower application level.
Emit effect values when changing an attribute and the bare keyword when restoring the inherited value. Keep paragraph attributes adjacent to the text/paragraph they control.
Use documented core syntax for portable output. If retaining opaque extensions, copy their complete brace-delimited form rather than attempting to reinterpret unknown arguments.

subsection.title: Self-contained styled text
subsection.p: A minimal portable file defines a style then applies and removes it.

p.extended-example: {define style Notice; font "Homerton.Bold"; fontsize 18pt; fontcolour rgb=(1,0,0)} {style Notice on}Important{style Notice off} ordinary text.{cr}

subsection.title: Paragraph ruler and effects
subsection.p: This uses a ruler, decimal tab and temporary italic effect.

subsection.title: Independent style removal
subsection.p: The first style may be removed while the second remains active. After the first off command, Emphasis still applies to second.
